metadata.note: The West Virginia Central and Pittsburg Railway -- Henry Gassaway Davis's railroad, and the reason Elkins, Davis, Thomas and Parsons exist as towns. Added 2026-08-27 by request. Davis held a charter from 1866 but began building only in April 1880, south from a B&O junction near Bloomington, Maryland up the North Branch Potomac; he reached the Elk Garden coal in 1881, took new charters under the WVC&P name, and formally opened the railroad on November 2 1881. From Elkins, reached in November 1889, four lines eventually radiated: north to Cumberland, west to Belington, south to Huttonsville, and east to Durbin over the Coal and Iron Railway. Davis sold the whole system to George Gould's Fuller Syndicate in 1902 and it was merged into the Western Maryland Railway in 1905, so every line here is drawn twice -- once in the WVC&P's colour to 1905 and once in the Western Maryland's afterwards, per CLAUDE.md Rule 4. Passenger service lasted until 1958 on the Cumberland-Elkins main line and until April 10 1959 on the Elkins-Durbin mixed train, which was the last passenger train the Western Maryland ran anywhere.
metadata.not_drawn: The Elk Garden Branch and the short Keyser Branch appear on the Wikipedia system map but are NOT drawn: they were built to reach coal, and nothing consulted says either carried passengers, so under CLAUDE.md Rule 1 they stay off the map. The Coal and Coke Railway, Davis's other railroad, ran from Elkins to Charleston and was a separate company outside the WVC&P system; it is not drawn here. The modern excursions are also not drawn, and that is a sourcing failure rather than a judgement: the West Virginia Central Railroad runs the New Tygart Flyer, the Cheat Mountain Salamander and the Mountain Explorer dinner train out of Elkins over this very trackage, which is exactly the tourist_rail service CLAUDE.md Rule 1 says belongs on the map, but no source consulted gives their routes or first seasons, and the place names they advertise (High Falls of Cheat, Cheat Bridge) geocode 4-5 km off the traced line, so drawing them would have been guesswork. The Durbin Rocket is a separate case: it runs on the ex-Chesapeake and Ohio Greenbrier Division, not on WVC&P rails at all.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: The end years on two of the five Western Maryland features -- Belington and Huttonsville -- are UPPER BOUNDS, not dates. The February 1952 Official Guide shows both branches as freight-only tables, which is why they end at 1951 rather than at the system-wide 1958; but nothing found says when their passenger trains actually stopped, and it could have been decades earlier. Read those two as 'no later than'. The other three end years are sourced: Cumberland-Elkins 1957-1958, the Davis Branch 1942 and the Elkins-Durbin mixed train April 10 1959. Headways and speeds on those two lines are now read off the September 30 1951 timetable rather than estimated; every other headway_min in this file is still an estimate; the one frequency figure that is real -- eighteen passenger trains a day at Elkins in 1930 -- was read directly from the West Virginia Railroad Museum entry, which attributes it to a source of its own that has not been chased. No total route mileage for the WVC&P system was found, so the traced lengths in this file are checked only against each other and against town positions, not against a documented figure. Whether the Davis Branch and the Elk Garden Branch carried scheduled passengers under the WVC&P is likewise undocumented in what was consulted; the Davis Branch is drawn on the reasoning that Davis was a town of some thousands at the end of it and that its depot is documented as a passenger stop; the Elk Garden Branch is not. WHAT WAS CHECKED AND WHAT IS LEFT: the February 1952 Official Guide has now been read -- archive.org holds a full scan -- and it settled a good deal: the 112.1 and 47.1 mile figures, the real 1951 timetable frequencies that replaced two estimated headways, the milepost-by-milepost check on the main line, and the proof that the Belington and Huttonsville branches were freight-only by then. What it cannot give is a DATE for those two, only a bound. Settling that needs an Official Guide from the 1920s, 1930s or 1940s -- archive.org has no other full volume and HathiTrust, which does, blocks automated fetches -- or ICC discontinuance dockets, or the two standard books, Clarke's The West Virginia Central and Pittsburg Railway (2003) and Salamon and Hopkins's The Western Maryland Railway in the Diesel Era (1991). None of those has been consulted, and Poor's Manual, which would give the system mileage, has not been read either. Read the remaining gaps as not-yet-looked-for, not as not-findable.

segments.note: Up the North Branch to its source, through Bayard and over Backbone Mountain: by November 1884 the line had reached Thomas -- the first train ran into the place, then called Fairfax, on August 10 1884 -- and by November the spot that became the town of Davis. Thomas and Davis turned into the centre of the operation -- logging, sawmills, tanning, and from the 1890s the Davis Coal and Coke Company, which was for a time among the largest coal producers in the country. Frequency estimated.

segments.note: The hardest piece of the railroad: down the Blackwater Canyon from Thomas to Hendricks, then along the Dry Fork and Shavers Fork through Parsons, reached in 1888, and up Leading Creek to a place then called Leadville. The rails got there in November 1889 and the first passenger train ran in on December 3 1889. The town was renamed Elkins for Davis's son-in-law and business partner Stephen B. Elkins, and became the hub from which the railroad's four lines radiated. Frequency estimated.

properties.geometry_quality: NOT traced by this repo from OpenStreetMap: 10.2 km (6.4 mi) taken directly from the Wikimedia Commons route map that backs the Wikipedia system diagram, at its own 156-point resolution (about 65 m between points, so it is a real trace rather than a sketch). It is used here because OpenStreetMap has almost nothing for this branch -- a corridor search finds only about 3.4 km of Blackwater Canyon Trail ways at the Thomas end, and the Davis end is unmapped, so a self-traced version was not possible. The drawn line touches the Thomas-Elkins trace to within 36 m at Thomas and passes 0.23 km from Davis, and is 6.4 mi long against the 6.3 miles the Thomas and Davis histories document -- the closest mileage agreement in this file, and a good check on geometry that is not this repo's own trace. Its shape is a U -- west out of Davis, dipping about 2 km south-west of Thomas, then hooking back north-east into the town -- which makes it 10.2 km long against a 4.3 km straight line. That is NOT a doubled-back routing artifact (no two points on it come within 100 m of each other); it is the grade working round the head of the Blackwater canyon and the coal works below Thomas. Provenance of the Commons data itself is not stated on the file page beyond its CC-BY-4.0 licence, but the mileage agreement is a good sign that it is the right line.

segments.note: Thomas and Davis are three miles apart across the Blackwater, and the railroad served both: the main line turned south-west at Thomas for the canyon while this branch ran on east to Davis, the town Henry Davis founded and named for himself and the terminus the line had reached in November 1884. Davis was a company town of sawmills, a tannery and the Davis Coal and Coke headquarters, and its people rode this branch to reach the main line. Frequency estimated.

segments.note: George Gould's Fuller Syndicate bought the WVC&P and its subsidiaries from Davis in 1902 and merged them into the Western Maryland in 1905; the new WM main line met the old West Virginia Central at Ridgeley, across the Potomac from Cumberland. This became the WM's route into the West Virginia coal and timber country, and Elkins its western hub -- by 1930 eighteen passenger trains a day were arriving at and leaving Elkins. The WM was a coal railroad that ran a small passenger operation on the side. Its September 30 1951 timetable, the last one printed in an Official Guide that this repo could read, still shows two trains each way daily except Sunday over the whole 112.1 miles, with individual-seat air-conditioned coaches: Nos. 1 and 9 down from Cumberland, Nos. 4 and 10 back up from Elkins. The WM gave up its Baltimore-Hagerstown main line trains in 1957 and this service between 1957 and 1958.
sources: Segment-level: the 1902 sale, the 1905 merger, the Ridgeley connection and the 1957-1958 end of Cumberland-Elkins passenger service are sourced; the two-trains-each-way frequency and the train numbers are read off the September 30 1951 timetable in the February 1952 Official Guide, and headway_min is that frequency, not an estimate; the 1930 figure of eighteen trains a day is quoted verbatim from the West Virginia Railroad Museum entry, which cites a source of its own for it that has not been chased.

segments.note: The Coal and Iron line became the Western Maryland's Durbin Subdivision in 1905, and it outlasted every other passenger train on the railroad. It was always a mixed train -- freight cars and a coach. In the February 1952 Official Guide it still ran daily except Sunday, out of Elkins at 11.05 am and into Durbin at 1.30 pm, where it handed passengers to the Chesapeake and Ohio's Greenbrier Division motor car at 1.40 pm for Marlinton and Ronceverte. By the end it had thinned to three days a week. It made its last trip on April 10 1959, which was the end of passenger service on the whole Western Maryland Railway. headway_min is the daily-except-Sunday frequency of the 1952 timetable, not an estimate.
